source_units.text: if they said, “Because I did not send him the money and the children, he perished.”
source_units.prior_reason: The imagined accusation against Simon explains his ransom decision, with no independently supported parallel to that specific accusation.

source_units.text: Tryphon prepared all his cavalry to go, but that night there was exceedingly heavy snow, and he did not go because of the snow. He set out and came to Gilead.
source_units.prior_reason: The snow-stopped cavalry journey and diversion to Gilead have no verified particular cross-reference in the passages read.

source_units.text: Tryphon turned and went away to his own land.
source_units.prior_reason: Tryphon's return home is a short travel notice; a common departure formula does not supply a substantive cross-reference.

source_units.text: King Demetrius sent to him in these words, replying with a letter of this form:
source_units.prior_reason: This introduction to Demetrius's letter supplies no substantive term beyond those individually reviewed in the following verses.

source_units.text: Those in the siege tower leaped into the city, and a great commotion arose in the city.
source_units.prior_reason: The siege-tower soldiers' entry and the city's commotion are specific tactical details not independently supplied by the later summary of Gazara's restoration.

source_units.text: Arsaces king of Persia and Media heard that Demetrius had entered his territory, and sent one of his commanders to seize him alive.
source_units.prior_reason: Arsaces's instruction to capture Demetrius alive has no independently verified parallel; shared royal names in the later recipient list are insufficient.

source_units.text: He went, struck Demetrius’s army, seized him, and brought him to Arsaces, who put him under guard.
source_units.prior_reason: The capture and imprisonment of Demetrius by Arsaces have no separately verified account in the passages read.

source_units.text: Those who fought them ceased from the land, and the kings were crushed in those days.
source_units.prior_reason: The panegyric's general claim that opposing kings were crushed does not identify a particular narrated defeat for a secure cross-reference.

source_units.text: The letters were read before the assembly in Jerusalem.
source_units.prior_reason: Public reading of these letters is a general documentary practice; no particular textual dependence on another public reading was established.

source_units.text: When the people heard these things, they said, “What thanks shall we return to Simon and his sons?
source_units.prior_reason: The rhetorical question about thanks introduces the following tribute and has no sufficiently specific independent target.

source_units.text: in a great assembly of priests, people, rulers of the nation, and elders of the country, a declaration was made to us:
source_units.prior_reason: The enumeration of assembly participants introduces the decree; a shared list of priests, people, and elders alone would be too general.

source_units.text: Whoever acts contrary to these provisions or annuls any of them shall be liable.’
source_units.prior_reason: The liability clause gives no particular penalty or law citation allowing a securely grounded external legal cross-reference.

source_units.text: and that copies be placed in the treasury so that Simon and his sons might possess them.”
source_units.prior_reason: Archival copies for Simon and his sons are specified here; no separate passage establishes this precise custody arrangement.

source_units.text: Antiochus son of King Demetrius sent letters from the islands of the sea to Simon, priest and ethnarch of the Jews, and to the whole nation.
source_units.prior_reason: After full triple rereading, the proposed link to later arrival was removed: sending letters from islands and later landing is routine sequencing, weaker than the explicit campaign intention and fulfilment retained at 15:4.

source_units.text: I permit you to strike your own coinage as money for your country.
source_units.prior_reason: The grant of coinage rights has no verified counterpart in the passages read; later coins or modern historical evidence are not substituted for a canonical target.

source_units.text: In the one hundred and seventy-fourth year Antiochus went out into the land of his fathers. All the forces joined him, so that only a few remained with Tryphon.
source_units.prior_reason: The arrival and mass accession of troops are retained as context for an explicit earlier intention, but no additional independently useful source-side link was established for this dated notice.

source_units.text: Antiochus pursued him, and he fled to Dora by the sea,
source_units.prior_reason: The pursuit and retreat to Dora are read as context for the campaign and subsequent escape; a second routine movement link is not added solely to cover this unit.

source_units.text: Antiochus encamped against Dora, with a hundred and twenty thousand warriors and eight thousand cavalry.
source_units.prior_reason: The siege's army figures have no independently verified parallel; the later resumptive account does not independently support those figures.

source_units.text: “Lucius, consul of the Romans, to King Ptolemy, greetings.
source_units.prior_reason: The Roman consul's greeting to King Ptolemy supplies no securely resolved identification with another named Ptolemy passage; a common royal name is not sufficient.

source_units.text: If, therefore, any pestilent men have escaped from their country to you, hand them over to Simon the high priest, so that he may punish them according to their law.”
source_units.prior_reason: The extradition request names no individual fugitive or specific legal provision, so neither earlier accusers nor an unspecific punishment law is forced into a target.

source_units.text: He wrote the same things to King Demetrius, Attalus, Ariarathes, and Arsaces,
source_units.prior_reason: The list of royal recipients does not itself establish substantive links to other episodes involving similarly named kings.

source_units.text: and to all the countries: to Sampsame, the Spartans, Delos, Myndos, Sicyon, Caria, Samos, Pamphylia, Lycia, Halicarnassus, Rhodes, Phaselis, Cos, Side, Aradus, Gortyna, Cnidus, Cyprus, and Cyrene.
source_units.prior_reason: The geographical recipient list supplies no specific narrated action in the named places to support an additional cross-reference.

source_units.text: They wrote a copy of these things to Simon the high priest.
source_units.prior_reason: The copy sent to Simon is a brief documentary notice; no separate text identifies this exact copy beyond its surrounding letter.

source_units.text: Athenobius, the king’s Friend, came to Jerusalem. He saw Simon’s glory, the display of gold and silver vessels, and the large retinue, and was astonished. He reported the king’s words to him.
source_units.prior_reason: Athenobius sees Simon's display vessels, but the sanctuary vessels in the earlier praise are not identified as the same objects; no object identity is forced.

source_units.text: He did not answer him a word, but returned angrily to the king and reported these words, Simon’s glory, and everything he had seen. The king became greatly angry.
source_units.prior_reason: The envoy's angry report and the king's anger continue the immediate negotiation, with no distinct substantive target beyond that local sequence.

source_units.text: They arose in the morning and went into the plain. A large force of infantry and cavalry came to meet them, with a stream between them.
source_units.prior_reason: The armies' positions beside an unnamed stream do not establish identity with another river or battle scene.

source_units.text: He divided the people, placing the cavalry among the infantry, for the adversaries had very many cavalry.
source_units.prior_reason: The placement of cavalry among infantry has no verified tactical counterpart; other cavalry battles do not establish this particular arrangement.

source_units.text: Ptolemy son of Abubus had been appointed commander over the plain of Jericho and possessed much silver and gold,
source_units.prior_reason: Ptolemy son of Abubus's command at Jericho and wealth have no separately verified parallel; other men named Ptolemy are not identified with him.

source_units.text: for he was the high priest’s son-in-law.
source_units.prior_reason: The relationship of Simon's son-in-law is not independently attested in the passages read; general hostile in-law narratives do not establish this genealogy.

source_units.text: Simon was visiting the cities in the country and attending to their care. He came down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas in the one hundred and seventy-seventh year, in the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat.
source_units.prior_reason: The dated visit to Jericho with Mattathias and Judas has no independently verified parallel; generic duties of government do not establish this particular journey.

source_units.text: Ptolemy wrote these things and sent them to the king, asking him to send forces to help him and hand over their country and cities.
source_units.prior_reason: Ptolemy's request for royal military aid and transfer of the country has no verified independent outcome or parallel beyond his immediate coup narrative.

source_units.text: He sent others to seize Jerusalem and the temple mountain.
source_units.prior_reason: The dispatch to seize Jerusalem and the temple mountain has no narrated outcome here; earlier residence on the mountain alone is insufficient for a separate connection.
